Plausible

/PLAW-zuh-bul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Plausible means seeming reasonable or believable, though not proven.

Plausible means seeming reasonable or believable, though not proven. Her excuse for missing practice was plausible: the bridge into town really had been closed for repairs all afternoon.

Worked Example

When the museum's prized vase turned up cracked, the intern offered an explanation that struck everyone as plausible: the janitor's cart had a squeaky, wobbling wheel, the display shelf sat slightly crooked, and the cleaning log showed the room had been mopped an hour earlier. No one could yet prove that a bump from the cart had done it, but the story fit the facts and seemed entirely reasonable to believe.

The intern's explanation seemed reasonable and believable even though it had not been proven, which is exactly what plausible means.

How Plausible Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

believable

believable: able to be accepted as true

credible

credible: convincing enough to be worthy of belief

Antonyms

far-fetched

far-fetched: too unlikely to be believed

implausible

implausible: not seeming reasonable or believable

How Strong Is It? — conceivable → plausible → convincing

conceivable vs. plausible

conceivable vs. plausible: A conceivable explanation is merely possible to imagine, while a plausible one actually seems reasonable and believable on its face.

convincing vs. plausible

convincing vs. plausible: A plausible account sounds believable, but a convincing one goes further and actually wins the listener over.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — plaus

Root — plaus: from Latin plaudere, to clap or applaud

Suffix — -ible

Suffix — -ible: able to be, worthy of

Put it together

Put it together: Plausible comes from Latin plausibilis, 'deserving applause,' built on plaudere, 'to clap.' A plausible explanation was originally one worth clapping for, one an audience would accept. The same root hides in explode, which first meant to clap and hoot a bad performer off the stage.

Use the root in a new word: plaudits

Use the root in a new word: plaudits: The young violinist earned the plaudits of the entire hall, applause in its most literal Latin sense, from the same root plaudere that builds plausible.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral, academic and everyday register

Plausible describes claims, explanations, theories, excuses, and stories, things people say or believe, and judges only how believable they sound, not whether they have been proven. Calling an account plausible stops well short of calling it true.
